body.text: Oil prices jumped 3 per cent to $US120/barrel, a level not seen since early in the US/Iran war.
That has seen risk assets like shares put under pressure, with key US indices all falling on Friday and the ASX set to follow today.

RBA's chief economist reinforces expectations of one more rate hike

The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter has done an interview on 60 Minutes, recorded on October 21 and aired last night, which has backed up much of what was said by the RBA's deputy governor Andrew Hauser at the Citi Investment Conference last week.

"You see what's going on overseas, it's nothing to do with you, it's nothing to do with us," Hunter said."We can't stop that, but what we can do, and we must do, is make sure it doesn't become embedded."We don't want to live with high inflation for a long time. We want to get it out of the system."
"You see what's going on overseas, it's nothing to do with you, it's nothing to do with us," Hunter said.
"We can't stop that, but what we can do, and we must do, is make sure it doesn't become embedded.
"We don't want to live with high inflation for a long time. We want to get it out of the system."
"So we're still talking about inflation being high. Haven't we done enough?" Asked interviewer Adam Hegarty.
"It's tricky. It is hard. Unfortunately, not quite yet," responded Hunter.
"Obviously, the board have put through four rate hikes this year to keep on tackling the challenge.

"So not quite yet, but we I do think, and we do know from history and from looking at other countries too, high higher interest rates, higher rates will work. They do get through the system, they do bring inflation down, but it does take a bit of time, and that's the challenge at the moment.
"We're just stuck where we are today. We're just looking and need a bit more time. But the rates do work. Higher rates do work."

Financial markets are seeing that as reinforcement of Hauser's message last week, with market pricing on a November rate hike at around two-thirds, with a rate hike fully priced in by February next year.
If it's any consolation to borrowers, markets are currently pricing in less than a 25% chance of two hikes.
Key Event
Why is gold losing its glitter?
As we noted earlier this morning, there is usually a positive correlation between rising oil prices and the price of gold.
So why with oil ripping higher to its highest level since April is gold now below $US4,000/ounce, its lowest level since July?
ANZ's commodities analyst Daniel Hynes points out the expectation of "tighter monetary policies" and rising interest rates is behind the move.
"A rotation out of AI-related stocks pushed investors toward the safety of US bonds…resulted in a rise in yields in US Treasuries, a headwind for non-yielding assets such as gold," Mr Hynes said.
Current market pricing points to the Fed leaving rates unchanged at this week's FOMC meeting, but a 78% chance of a December hike.

"Heightened inflation concerns suggest that major central banks of the world won't be able to ease monetary policies as quickly as they want to. All that's working against the gold and silver market bulls at present," American Gold Exchange analyst Jim Wyckoff told Reuters.
Mr Wyckoff also noted the selloff in technology stocks has also led to margin calls for equity traders and investors, prompting them to sell gold and silver assets.
Operation Jawbone's dislocation
"I guess I should warn you, if I turn out to be particularly clear, you've probably misunderstood what I said." Dr Alan Greenspan, former US Federal Reserve chair.
Oh, for the good old days of central banking, when every word was a lesson in obfuscation.

"Fedspeak" aka "Greenspeak", coined in honour of the good doctor, was a weapon of mass distraction to prevent financial markets overreacting, or indeed reacting at all, to public comments from Dr Greenspan.
One of his critics, former Princeton economics professor and Fed vice chair to Dr Greenspan for a while, Alan Binder called Fedspeak "a turgid dialect of English".
But that's a whole different story, which may not explain what Dr Greenspan was getting at, as much as Professor Binder's shorter-than-expected tenure at the Fed.
These days, central bankers have developed a bit of market moving clarity. It's deliberate.
It's also known as "jawboning", a process where central bankers' commentary works as a proxy for actually pulling interest rate levers.
However, central bank leaders can still simultaneously send the market in different directions, while trying to "keep on message".

To wit, RBA governor Michelle Bullock and her Deputy, the loquacious Andrew Hauser seem to have sparked totally different reactions to their comments after the board's unanimous and "hawkish" 25 basis point hike to 4.60%.
The CBA's economic team has published an interesting minute-by-minute analysis of the market's reaction to recent speeches by Governor Bullock and Deputy Governor Hauser.
On October 21, Dr Hauser sent the market's pricing for a November hike higher. On September 29, Ms Bullock sent the pricing lower.

"Governor Bullock's post-meeting press conference struck a softer tone, emphasising the long lags in monetary policy and the cumulative impact of the four hikes delivered this year," CBA economist Harry Ottley said.
"November pricing fell by around 4bp during the appearance."

"Deputy Governor Hauser's intervention (last week) moved expectations sharply in the opposite direction. He described the inflation outlook as 'materially worse' than projected in August, said upside inflation risks had crystallised and characterised the Board as facing "hard choices" between persistent inflation and weaker activity and employment
"Markets consequently priced around 3 — 4bp more tightening."
So, which is it? Who knows, but somewhere up there, Alan Greenspan is probably looking down at the RBA's jawboning efforts with an enigmatic smile.

But yes, CME copper was up 1.8% to $US6.48/pound and Shanghai Futures Exchange copper was up 0.1% to 107.79 yuan/tonne and a morning note from NAB's market team quotes the LME price as up 1.8% to $US14,098/tonne — so you may well have a point.
US reporting season hits overdrive
Wall Street is facing a pivotal week in its Q3 results season with a deluge of numbers due with around one third of the S&P500 cohort reporting.
That includes updates from the likes of Alphabet (AKA Google), Microsoft (both Wednesday) and Amazon (Thursday).
Chip companies Intel and Sandisk could also influence sentiment in the AI trade.
So far things have been positive despite disappointments from the likes Meta and semi-conductor maker Lam last week.
With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 30% from a year ago.
"There are a lot of balls in the air," Alpine Macro chief equity strategist Nick Giorgi told Reuters
"Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence.

"The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain."
Other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lill, oil majors Exxon and Chevron and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar.

Locally, the key event of the week will be the Q3 CPI from the ABS on Wednesday.
The market consensus is that the headline inflation rate will be 1.3% over the quarter, up from 0.6%, but will hold the annual pace flat at 3.9%.
The RBA's preferred Trimmed Mean measure is expected to come in at 0.6% over the quarter is forecast to edge up to around 1.o%, which would also see the annual hold at 3.6%.

"If realised, this would mark the fifth consecutive quarter in which trimmed mean inflation has increased by between 0.8% and 1.0%, highlighting the persistence of underlying inflation pressures," CBA's economics team wrote in a weekend note.

"The outcome would also be above the RBA's August forecast for trimmed mean inflation of around 0.8%/qtr, although the strength of the July and August monthly CPI prints means some deterioration in the inflation outlook is already well understood by the Board."
There will be another important insight into inflation with Friday's release of the Q3 Producers' Price Index.

"Final demand prices rose 1.3%/qtr and 3.6%/yr in Q2, the strongest quarterly increase since September 2023, with higher energy, freight and construction costs prominent," CBA said."The Q3 release will therefore be useful for assessing whether recent energy and supply chain pressures are continuing to lift upstream inflation."
"Final demand prices rose 1.3%/qtr and 3.6%/yr in Q2, the strongest quarterly increase since September 2023, with higher energy, freight and construction costs prominent," CBA said.
"The Q3 release will therefore be useful for assessing whether recent energy and supply chain pressures are continuing to lift upstream inflation."

Around the time the CPI figures drop on Wednesday, RBA Governor Michelle Bullock and her key lieutenants will be fronting the Senate Estimates Committee in Canberra, so we may get a real time reaction to the data.
Overseas, the focus will be on interest rate decisions from some of the biggest and most influential central banks.

The biggest and most influential, the US Federal Reserve makes its call on Thursday and is expected to keep its powder dry with a number of key voting members suggesting they are not in a hurry to lift rates again soon.
The Bank of Canada will follow soon after and it too is expected to be on hold, although a split decision is expected.

The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan on Friday are also expected to be on hold, although the BoJ's guidance has not been that clear, and both are tipped to make another hike before the end of the year.
New Zealand's central bank is expected to lift its cash rate on Wednesday 25bp to 3.0%.
The big economies will also publish Q3 GDP numbers. Solid consumer spending and AI investment should see US GDP growth holding up at 3.4% (YoY).
The EU is expected to report a 0.3% jump in GDP over the quarter, following on from solid growth of 0.6% in Q2.

Another one to watch will the first UK budget brought down by new Prime Minister Andy Burham. His Chancellor John Healy has said that he will stick to the current fiscal rules and aims to deliver "a buffer also for uncertainty".
Key Event
Wall Street slips on oil, ASX to open lower
Wall Street's major indices all closed lower on Friday, although it wasn't AI stocks doing all the damage this time.
Global oil prices jumping another 3% to their highest level since April certainly helped fuel the general retreat.
• Nasdaq: -0.2%
Tech stocks were among the steadier performers amid widespread wobbles.
The Nasdaq's narrow loss was an improvement on Thursday's dump when the index endured is biggest fall since June as investors continued to fret about spending and investment returns in the sector.
Those anxieties remain, it's just that oil and inflation were the session's bigger worries
The S&P 500 energy sector, however, was resolute, gaining another 2.5% to another record high as key oil indices rose to levels last seen early in the US/Iran war.
• Brent futures: +3.1% to $US116.72/barrel
• WTI futures: +3.8% to $U103.27/barrel
That wave of worry will again likely wash up on our shores with futures trading pointing to a 0.5% decline on the ASX 200 this morning.
For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain.
Telecommunications stocks fell again on Friday, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.
Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.
Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year.
S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

This week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched by investors.
US Treasury yields rose, a day after the benchmark 10-year yield saw its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years but remained around the 5% mark.
Gold fell to a three-month low as higher energy prices fuelled inflation concerns and reinforced US rate hike expectations ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting.
It gave up 4% over the week, and is now below $US4,000/ounce for the first time since July. The move also signalled a break from gold's usual positive correlation with oil.
